newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS-Grolsch profit up on one-off gain,1997 bleak.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Grolsch profit up on one-off gain,1997 bleak.

text.p: Dutch brewer Grolsch reported a meagre 1.8 percent rise in 1996 profit on Wednesday as increasing competition in a stagnant market and a poor summer took their toll.
Grolsch also forecast a lower profit in the current year because of a one-off gain in 1996.

The company said net profit in 1996 was 59.9 million guilders ($31.1 million), versus 58.8 million in 1995, but the latest result included a six million guilder after-tax gain related to a co-operation agreement with a foreign party.
In response to the result, which was below expectations, and the gloomy outlook, Grolsch shares tumbled by 13.30 guilders, or 18 percent, to stand at 60.70 guilders at 1320 GMT.
Chairman Paul Snoep told a news conference the north-west European beer markets had shown signs of saturation since 1990, with beer sales levelling off.
"Competition intensified as a result, and a growth market turned into one with brewers struggling for market share, placing a certain amount of pressure on margins," he said.
Operating results rose 7.8 percent to 95.4 million guilders, including the incidental gain.
Grolsch said the first half of 1996 was good but the second half was a disappointment.
"The summer weather of 1996 was very mediocre compared to the tropical summer of 1995," it said.
It said exports rose in 1996, but it was accompanied by a significant rise in costs, notably sales and personnel.
Turnover rose 7.3 percent to 676.8 million guilders, helped by organic growth, a larger stake in Poland and the purchase of two liquor traders in the Netherlands.
The company also said it expected 1997 results to be lower because of the one-off gain in 1996.
But Snoep later told reporters he expected 1997 profit would rise if this item was excluded from the 1996 results.
"I expect that 1997 profit compared with 1996, if you strip out incidentals, will show a rising trend," he said.
He said the gain came from an agreement with a party outside the Netherlands that distributed Grolsch but which did not want to reveal its identity.
"This is part of the latent value of the Grolsch brand. We are planting seeds in several countries," Snoep said.
Snoep did not expect incidental gains in 1997 but added there was a chance of similar gains in later years.
Exports rose more than the national turnover in 1996.
Snoep said the German beer market increasingly became subject to a price war but Grolsch's presence in Germany was, and would remain, modest.
He said the beer market in Poland was becoming more concentrated, with five parties currently accounting for over 60 percent of production.
"We are the market-leader, twice as big as the next brand, and will benefit from this trend," he said.
He also said there did not appear to be any way to stop the downward trend in the British beer market.
In Britain, Grolsch owns the Ruddles Brewery and is active through a joint venture with Bass Plc.
The company said it saw insufficient room in several important beer markets to raise selling prices in 1997.
But it expected to hold its strong market position in the Netherlands and gain from contributions from its Polish unit and rising exports.
Currency effects were also expected to be more favourable than in 1996.
($ = 1.924 Dutch Guilders)
